passage_text: Researchers studied the effects of a new insulin analog on glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. Eighty participants were randomized to receive either the analog or a standard insulin formulation for 28 days. Blood glucose levels were measured fasting and 2 hours postprandially on days 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, and 28. Insulin doses were adjusted weekly to maintain target fasting glucose < 140 mg/dL. Body weight was recorded at each visit. The study aimed to determine whether the analog could reduce postprandial excursions while minimizing weight gain. The following table summarizes the key measurements in the analog group at baseline (day 0) and day 28.
stem: Which statement best describes the changes in the analog group from day 0 to day 28?

options.A: Fasting glucose fell but postprandial glucose did not change.
options.B: Fasting and postprandial glucose both fell, and the daily insulin dose was lower.
options.D: None of the measured values changed.

explanation: Correct: fasting glucose fell 145 to 138 mg/dL, postprandial glucose 210 to 180 mg/dL, and dose 35 to 32 units/day. Why the others are wrong: A) Postprandial glucose also fell (210 to 180 mg/dL). C) Weight fell from 82.5 to 81.0 kg. D) Every measured value changed.
trap: Noticing the improvement in fasting glucose and overlooking the postprandial change.

stem: To attribute the changes in Table 1 to the analog rather than to insulin therapy in general, which additional data are most needed?

options.A: Day 0 and day 28 values for the standard-insulin group
options.B: Extra glucose readings in the analog group between days 0 and 28
options.C: The ages of the analog-group participants
options.D: The analog group's weight at every visit

explanation: Correct: a comparison group is needed to judge whether the changes exceed those with standard insulin. Why the others are wrong: B) More analog-only readings cannot show what standard insulin would have done. C) Age describes participants but provides no comparison. D) More weight data describe the analog group only.
trap: Adding more data from the same group instead of a comparator.

stem: Estimate the percent reduction in postprandial glucose from day 0 to day 28.
trap: Dividing the 30 mg/dL fall by the day-28 value (180) or mixing in the fasting values, instead of dividing by the day-0 postprandial value of 210 mg/dL.

stem: Which of the following conclusions is NOT supported by Table 1?

options.A: The daily insulin dose was lower at day 28 than at day 0.
options.B: Fasting glucose was lower at day 28 than at day 0.
options.C: The absolute fall in postprandial glucose exceeded the absolute fall in fasting glucose.
options.D: The analog caused greater weight loss than standard insulin.

explanation: Correct: Table 1 gives no data for standard insulin, so no comparison of weight loss is possible. Why the others are wrong: A) 35 to 32 units/day is a decrease. B) 145 to 138 mg/dL is a decrease. C) 30 mg/dL exceeds 7 mg/dL.
trap: Reading a before-after change in one group as a difference between treatments.

stem: Rapid-acting insulin analogs such as lispro and aspart lower postprandial glucose excursions primarily because of which property?

options.A: Amino acid substitutions reduce hexamer formation, so they dissociate and are absorbed faster from subcutaneous tissue.
options.B: They bind the insulin receptor with much higher affinity than human insulin.
options.C: They are given intravenously and bypass absorption.
options.D: They block glucagon release from alpha cells.

explanation: Rapid-acting analogs have sequence changes that weaken self-association into hexamers, so they dissociate to monomers quickly after injection, giving faster onset and shorter duration that match mealtime glucose rises.
trap: Option B: the receptor affinity of lispro and aspart is similar to human insulin; the difference is absorption kinetics.
